summary: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It builds on RFC 919 and humorously proposes sending broadcast packets over an alternative link layer that uses the atmosphere. It is satire and not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke where the internet's messages travel through the air in a silly way to reach many places at once. Nobody is meant to build it for real.

questions: what is an atmospheric link layer
how does skytyping work in rfc 6217
subtitle: An April 1st joke proposing skywriting to broadcast network messages.

tldr.problem: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It humorously claims that broadcasting network packets over the internet is inefficient and proposes using the atmosphere as an alternative physical link layer.
tldr.mechanism: Messages are transmitted by hiring aircraft to write in the sky using smoke signals, displayed in dot-matrix style at altitudes of 7,000 to 17,000 feet. Recipients optically scan the skywritten message and decode it into network packets.
tldr.outcome: The document is satire. It proposes a protocol (ADVERT: Asynchronous Dumb Visual Exchange of Raw Transmissions) and explains how to encode broadcast data as readable smoke letters in the sky, while acknowledging limitations like weather and line of sight. No actual implementation exists.

today: RFC 6217 is an April 1st joke RFC proposing skywriting as a broadcast link layer. It was published on 1 April 2011 and is not intended for implementation. The document is satire that humorously applies real networking concepts to an absurd physical medium.

sections.title: The Joke
sections.content:
This document is an April 1st RFC published on April 1, 2011. It proposes a humorous alternative link layer for broadcasting network packets: the Earth's atmosphere. The joke builds on RFC 919 (Broadcast Datagrams), which defines how to broadcast packets on a local network. RFC 6217 takes the concept to absurd extremes, proposing to replace Ethernet or other physical link layers with skywriting.

The author, T. Ritter, presents the atmosphere as a physical medium composed of nitrogen, oxygen, and trace elements, arguing that it is widely available in all major cities and rural locations. The punchline is that the proposed transmission method involves hiring aircraft to write messages in the sky using smoke, which recipients then optically read and manually type into their computers.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC jokes that the internet should send broadcast messages by having airplanes write them in the sky with smoke, and people look up and type them into their computers.

sections.title: The Proposed Protocol
sections.content:
The RFC defines ADVERT (Asynchronous Dumb Visual Exchange of Raw Transmissions), a network protocol designed for the atmospheric link layer. Unlike IPv4 or IPv6, which include fields for destination addresses and TTL, ADVERT strips these down to two simple fields: Content (the actual message) and Source (the sender's identifier—IP address, phone number, email, URI, or geographic address).

For human-readable messages, content is simply written in the sky as plain text. For machine-readable data (like an HTTP request), the RFC humorously specifies that UDP packets should be encoded in Base64 and written in the sky. An example in the document shows a broadcast HTTP request: GET / HTTP/1.1 encoded as R0VUIC8gSFRUUC8xLjENCg0K and displayed in the sky, with a source address of 203.0.113.8.
sections.plainLanguage: The made-up protocol says: write the message in the sky, and sign it with who you are. If it is plain text, write it readable. If it is a computer command, write it in a special code.

sections.title: Transmission and Reception
sections.content:
Messages are transmitted by emitting specialized smoke from aircraft at altitudes between 7,000 and 17,000 feet. The RFC suggests using a skytyping method similar to dot-matrix printing, which produces letters in a pixelated style and provides better persistence against air currents. The document notes that large organizations can hire specialized skywriting companies or, for frequent use, develop their own methods.

Reception is equally humorous: recipients must optically scan the skywritten datagram and convert it into an electronically transmittable form. Checksums, if present, should be computed and compared. If a checksum does not match, the packet must be discarded—the same rule as for any network protocol.

The RFC acknowledges serious limitations: weather conditions, line of sight, sleep patterns, and distraction may cause hosts to miss packets. Adversity like clouds or darkness may preclude transmission for extended periods. These limitations are presented matter-of-factly alongside genuine network protocol considerations, adding to the humor.
sections.plainLanguage: Airplanes write the message in smoke at high altitude. People look up, read it, and type it into their computers. Bad weather means the message is not readable.

sections.title: Practical and Humorous Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is careful to address both the joke and genuine protocol principles. It notes that data link layers are unnecessary for broadcast transmission and that implementers MUST NOT encapsulate packets in a link layer protocol. For plain-text content, no transport layer is needed; the message is simply embedded in ADVERT. For binary data, UDP SHOULD be used with Base64 encoding.

A particularly funny section addresses security: the RFC warns that organizations must be aware of accepting data from unknown senders and should use host-protection mechanisms and egress filtering. It also references RFC 1087, which classifies destruction of computer information as unethical, to argue that network operators should not silently discard skywritten datagrams.

The document concludes by discussing atmospheric conditions that affect transmission: moisture, ice crystals, and solar radiation all impact the reliability of the link layer. Regional operators should understand their local operating conditions and plan for the feasibility of implementing casual or robust infrastructure—a deadpan observation that fits the joke perfectly.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke includes serious-sounding rules about how networks should work, applied to skywriting. It even says network operators should not ignore skywritten messages.
